I'm a 42-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with a university degree, and I've been farming these ten mu of alluvial land on the North China Plain long enough to know what works. Our county is famous for the wheat-maize double-cropping system, and I'm not about to abandon a rotation that matches our climate and soil perfectly. I manage my land intensively but scientifically.

This spring, the winter wheat I sowed last October is greening up. I will topdress nitrogen at the reviving stage and irrigate three times in total—once now at green-up/jointing, once at heading, and once during grain filling. I use an improved semi-dwarf wheat variety that gives stable, high yields without lodging. Before last autumn's wheat sowing, I used rotary tillage to break up the stubble and create a fine seedbed. For nutrients, I apply 16 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium per mu, which is based on the soil test I did two years ago and the recommendations from the county extension station. I'll spray three times: a herbicide early in the spring, then a fungicide at heading to protect against Fusarium head blight, and another fungicide during filling to prevent rust. I expect about 580 kg per mu from this wheat crop.

Immediately after wheat harvest in early June, I will plant summer maize using no-tillage direct seeding. We only have a narrow window—maybe seven to ten days—between wheat harvest and the maize sowing deadline, so saving those two or three days by avoiding tillage is critical. I always buy certified hybrid maize seeds; I never save my own because hybrid vigor is lost in the second generation. I will irrigate twice—once around the jointing stage and once at filling—and rely on summer rainfall for the rest. Fertilizer rates will be 15 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, applied partly as base and partly as side-dressing. I will spray twice: a herbicide shortly after emergence and an insecticide at the trumpet stage to control corn borer. With good weather, I expect 650 kg per mu from the maize.

As someone with a university education, I follow the research coming out of China Agricultural University's station right here in Quzhou. I know groundwater is declining, so I don't waste water by over-irrigating, and I know over-fertilization damages soil structure without increasing yield. My annual plan is simple: optimize the standard double-cropping system rather than gamble on unfamiliar cash crops. This pays my children's school fees and leaves enough grain to sell to the state procurement station at a guaranteed minimum price.
